entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Born Girolamo Masci in Lisciano, Nicholas IV served as head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 22 February 1288 until his death on 4 April 1292, marking him as the first Franciscan friar to ascend to the papacy. His pontificate, though brief, was characterized by an intense, albeit ultimately unsuccessful, focus on organizing a new Crusade to the Holy Land following the escalating loss of Crusader territories, alongside significant diplomatic engagement with Eastern powers and a consistent patronage of his beloved Franciscan order and Roman artistic endeavors. His election represented a pivotal moment for the mendicant orders, solidifying their influence at the highest echelons of the Church.

During his four-year tenure, Nicholas IV prioritized the recovery of the Holy Land, dispatching legates across Europe to preach a new Crusade and levy taxes for its funding, efforts largely undermined by internal European conflicts, particularly the War of the Sicilian Vespers. He engaged in extensive correspondence with Mongol leaders, notably Arghun Khan of the Ilkhanate, exploring potential alliances against the Mamluks, and sent missionaries like John of Montecorvino to the Far East. Domestically, he reformed the administration of the Papal States and was a generous patron of the arts, commissioning significant works for Santa Maria Maggiore, including the mosaics by Jacopo Torriti depicting the Coronation of the Virgin, and overseeing improvements to the Lateran Palace.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nicholas IV significantly elevated the Franciscan order's standing within the Catholic Church and pursued ambitious, though ultimately unsuccessful, diplomatic efforts to revive the Crusader movement. His artistic patronage also left a lasting cultural footprint on Roman basilicas.
